definition: In computer programming, mutability refers to the ability of an object to be changed after it has been instantiated.
details: In computer programming, mutability refers to the ability of an object to be changed after it has been instantiated. Mutable objects have their fields and states changeable, while immutable objects do not allow any alteration after creation.

explainer.lead: Mutability is the ability of an object to be changed after it has been instantiated. It matters because mutable state is a common source of bugs when data is shared across code.

tiers.eli5: A mutable object is a whiteboard you can erase and rewrite; an immutable one is a printed page you can only replace.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers choose immutable objects for values shared across threads or used as keys, and mutable ones for accumulators. A pitfall is mutating an object that other code still references, causing unexpected changes elsewhere.
tiers.paperLevel: An object is mutable if its fields and state can change after creation; immutable objects allow no alteration after creation. Immutability guarantees stable identity of contents but requires copying to update.

explainer.example: A list used as a dictionary key is mutated, breaking lookups; switching to an immutable tuple fixes it.
